content.content:
# Product page: Trail Runner 2

A product page for our new trail running shoe, Trail Runner 2, on the Stride online store. The store is already a React app with a homepage that links to `/products/trail-runner-2`; build the product page at that address, using mock data, and don't add any packages to the app beyond React and its build tool. For the look, you can take inspiration from this design:

![Trail Runner 2 product page](design.jpg)

- **Store:** the shopper sees the store name and how many items are in their cart.
- **Search:** the shopper can type a product name, see matching suggestions as they type, move through them and choose one.
- **Menu:** the shopper can move through the store's main sections, such as men, women and kids, from the top of the page; opening a section shows its subsections, which they can move into and back out of.
- **Path:** the shopper sees where the shoe sits in the store, such as Shop, Trail, Trail Runner 2, and can go back to any earlier step.
- **Photos:** the shopper sees one photo of the shoe at a time as the photos advance automatically; they can pause or resume them and move to the next or previous one, going back to the first after the last.
- **Price:** the shopper sees the price and can point at a small "i" next to it to learn that it includes taxes.
- **Color:** the shopper can choose blue, black or grey; only the chosen color shows until they change it, each with a round swatch.
- **Size:** the shopper picks one size from a list that only opens when they want to change it; only the chosen size shows, and sold-out sizes can't be picked.
- **Store availability:** the shopper sees nearby stores as rows and sizes as columns, moves through the choices and picks an available store-and-size combination for pickup.
- **Size guide:** the shopper can open a size chart over the page from next to the size, enter their foot length and choose US or EU to get their size, and must close it to continue.
- **Quantity:** the shopper can choose how many pairs to buy, typing the number or changing it by one.
- **Delivery date:** the shopper opens a calendar, moves between days and months, and chooses an available delivery date; the chosen date is then shown on the page.
- **Add to cart:** the shopper adds the shoe to the cart and sees a confirmation; without a size they are asked to pick one.
- **Wishlist:** the shopper can save or unsave the shoe with a heart.
- **More information:** details, reviews and shipping sit side by side below everything, with one section shown at a time.
- **Questions:** a few common questions about the shoe, each with its answer hidden until the shopper opens it.
- **Bottom of the page:** the shopper finds customer help, company and social media links.
----

content.text:
The Red phase is in place. The suite has 103 Playwright tests in `tests/`. Against the empty product page, 102 fail and 1 passes. The passing one checks `lang="en"`, which `index.html` already sets, so it isn't a product-page test.

Run it with `npm test`. It takes about 9 minutes on this 2-CPU machine.

**What I added**
- `src/pages/ProductPage.jsx`: returns `null`, so the page is empty.
- `src/main.jsx`: one line routing `/products/trail-runner-2` to that page.
- `playwright.config.js`: Chromium only, starts the Vite dev server, and sets 5-second action and expect timeouts so failures show quickly.
- `tests/`: one spec per requirement group (`header`, `product-options`, `purchase`, `content`, `accessibility`), plus `helpers.js`.

**WCAG 2.2 AA and APG coverage**
- Every widget has a WCAG 2.2 AA axe scan. Scans of open states (search suggestions, menu, tooltip, size list, size guide, calendar) run where the state applies.
- Each widget is tested against its APG pattern: combobox, disclosure menu, carousel, tooltip, radio group, select-only combobox, grid, dialog, date picker, toggle button, tabs, and accordion. This covers roles, states, keyboard behavior, and focus management.
- Page-wide checks: landmarks, one `h1`, page title, skip link, visible focus on every tab stop, focus not obscured, and reflow at 320px.
- Whole-page and widget scans are guarded so they can't pass on the empty page.

**Decision for you: test tooling vs. "no packages beyond React and its build tool"**
I added `@playwright/test` and `@axe-core/playwright` as dev dependencies. Neither ships in the app bundle, but they are packages beyond React and Vite. Axe is what makes the WCAG 2.2 AA scan automated. If you want to keep it out, I'd drop axe and check those criteria by hand.

**Assumptions the Green phase must match**
The requirements don't name controls, so I chose the names and roles the tests look for. The main ones:
- Size is a select-only combobox with no size pre-selected. Sold-out options use `aria-disabled="true"`, and at least one must exist.
- Color is a radio group with swatches marked `data-testid="swatch"`. I read "only the chosen color shows" as one chosen color, with the photo alt text reflecting it.
- Store availability is a grid with regular rows and columns, and unavailable cells use `aria-disabled`.
- Quantity buttons are named "Increase quantity" and "Decrease quantity".
- The carousel uses a fake clock, so timing is deterministic.
- Search for "Trail" returns at least two suggestions.
- Some tests check whether a test passes or fails by reading `aria-*` attributes or element positions.

**Not covered**
Chromium only. Criteria that need manual review, such as text spacing and real screen reader output, are not tested. I haven't run the tests against a real implementation, so I can't yet say whether they are flaky.
